title: From Notification to Completion: Rethinking Reminder Systems for People Living with Dementia
hook: Why do reminders fail people living with dementia? This study names four interconnected phenomena (notification ephemerality, habituation, amnesia, and fatigue) and calls for reminder systems that support follow-through, not just notification.
authors: Stephen Becker, Susmitha Gurram, Alisha Pradhan, Emma Dixon
venue: ASSETS '26: The 28th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility · Vila Nova de Gaia, Portugal
about:
Reminder systems are among the most common technologies built for people living with dementia. Yet most of that work asks whether a reminder got the task done, not how people living with dementia actually experience the notifications themselves.

Through iterative interviews, six people living with mild to moderate dementia described what really happens when a reminder arrives. Four interconnected phenomena kept getting in the way:
• Notification ephemerality: reminders vanish before there's time to take them in.
• Notification habituation: the same reminder, seen day after day, stops registering.
• Notification amnesia: a reminder is read, then forgotten before anyone acts on it.
• Notification fatigue: so many reminders pile up that people tune them all out.

Keeping reminders working took a lot of invisible work: paper checklists by the front door, sticky notes on door handles, smartwatch buzzes, alarms set again and again. When a reminder still slipped by, many participants blamed themselves.

So what would a better reminder look like? Participants imagined AI-powered reminders that adapt how and when they notify, escalate when ignored, and help see a task through to completion. Drawing on mediation theory, the paper reimagines reminders as immersive systems that share responsibility for follow-through, and weighs what that means for monitoring and surveillance. Read it to see where the next generation of reminder technology could go.

title: Used By, Not Used On: An Adaptive Systems Framework to Design Technology for and with People with Dementia
hook: To design adaptive systems for people with MCI or dementia as their abilities change, we proposed four user-configurable modules that keep people with dementia as primary decision-makers over what a system senses, infers, does, and how it communicates.
authors: Susmitha Gurram, Massa Belal, Shivansh Dutta, Emma Dixon, Alisha Pradhan
venue: CSCW '26 Companion: ACM Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work and Social Computing · Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
about:
Adaptive systems can support people living with MCI or dementia as their abilities change over time. But when a system senses behavior, infers needs, or acts on someone's behalf, it can also cross boundaries around privacy, autonomy, and control. HCI offers established ways to reason about adaptive systems, from context-aware computing to mixed-initiative interaction, automation, and notification design, yet little work connects them to designing technology for and with people with dementia.

This framework brings them together into four user-configurable modules, keeping people with dementia as the primary decision-makers:
• Sensing/system input scope, what the system knows: from only what you tell it, all the way to patterns in your routine.
• Inference scope, what it may conclude: only what you wrote, or its own inferences.
• Assistance authority, how far it may go: suggestion-only, confirmed action, or autonomous action.
• Output delivery strategy, how it communicates: always the same way, or adapting its timing, channel, and modality.

A single leaving-home reminder shows the range. A pressure-sensing doormat can simply say "take your keys and wallet" without knowing who you are. Or the system can recognize you, check your calendar and the weather, and suggest a rain jacket for the community garden. Or, if you don't respond, it can turn firmer and send a text. Same moment, very different levels of privacy and help.

The framework is built for people living with MCI or dementia, but the questions it asks (what should a system sense, infer, do, and say, and who decides?) are ones anyone designing adaptive technology will face. Read the poster to see how existing assistive technologies map onto the framework.

title: Analysis of Wavelet, Ridgelet and Curvelet Transforms on Image Denoising
hook: A comparative study of wavelet, ridgelet, and curvelet transforms for image denoising, identifying the curvelet transform as the strongest fit for medical imaging.
authors: Susmitha Gurram, U. B. S. Chagantipati
venue: International Research Journal of Engineering and Technology (IRJET), Vol. 8, Issue 12, pp. 1066–1073
about:
Denoising has to remove noise without erasing the edges and contours that carry an image's meaning, a trade-off that matters most in medical imaging. This study implemented and compared three multiscale transforms, wavelet, ridgelet, and curvelet, in MATLAB, evaluating how well each suppressed noise while preserving image detail.

Wavelets capture point-like detail well and ridgelets capture straight lines, while curvelets are designed to represent curved edges. The curvelet transform delivered the best results, improving signal-to-noise ratio by about 20%, which makes it the strongest choice of the three for medical imaging.

title: 3D-MIMO with Massive Antennas in 5G Technology
hook: Arranging 64 or more antennas in a two-dimensional grid lets 5G base stations steer beams vertically as well as horizontally. This paper examines how 3D-MIMO raises capacity and reduces interference.
venue: International Research Journal of Engineering and Technology (IRJET), Vol. 8, Issue 3
about:
5G networks need far more capacity than today's systems, and one way to get it is to equip base stations with massive numbers of antennas, 64, 128, or more. Lined up horizontally, that many antennas would make panels impractically large. Arranging them in a two-dimensional grid, known as 3D-MIMO, keeps panels compact and lets beams be steered both horizontally and vertically.

This paper reviews 3D-MIMO with massive antennas: how 3D beamforming reduces intercell interference compared with traditional 2D beamforming, how multi-user MIMO serves more users at once, and where it applies, such as macro- and micro-cell coverage. It reports system-level simulation results in which 3D-MIMO with 64 antennas raises cell-average throughput by 117% and cell-edge throughput by 228%, and compares downlink precoding for single-user and multi-user MIMO transmission.
